page_header: Section A — Very Short Answer Question

steps.label: The definition
lines: The most probable speed of a gas is the speed
possessed by the maximum number of molecules
in the given sample of the gas.
It is the peak of the Maxwell speed distribution.
steps.why: Molecular speeds are spread over a range, and the spread has a peak. The speed at that peak — the one held by more molecules than any other single speed — is the most probable speed.
common_mistakes: Calling it the highest speed in the sample. It is the most COMMON speed, and it is the smallest of the three named speeds.
Confusing it with the average speed.
steps.memory_tip: Most probable = most common: the speed the largest number of molecules share.
steps.margin_note: The phrase maximum number of molecules is the marked wording.

steps.why: The factor under the root is 2 — smaller than the average speed's 8/π and the RMS speed's 3 — which is why the most probable speed is the smallest of the three.
common_mistakes: Writing 3RT under the root. The 3 belongs to the RMS speed; most probable takes 2.
Dropping the unit when a numerical follows — the speed comes out in m s⁻¹ with SI inputs.
steps.memory_tip: Two for the most probable, three for RMS: the smaller number under the root gives the smaller speed.
steps.margin_note: The 0.8165 line gives the ratio of the most probable speed to the RMS speed, which a paper may ask for on its own.

insider_note: Asked in March 2011 in exactly these words — the marked pair is the phrase maximum number of molecules plus √(2RT/M).
